name: Vera Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms or government, and your answers stay confidential. What is a normal working day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the loader crew at a large mine. I walk the bench before the first machine starts, check the maintenance sheet and spend much of the shift in a loader cab or helping another operator through a snag. I like seeing a new hand learn a difficult cut; I dislike being rushed by a schedule drawn by someone who has not seen the ground.

say: I say **loader work** still needs a careful operator even if reports fill themselves in.
I would judge an **automatic report** against what the crew sees on the machine.
think: I do not need **AI tools** to keep doing this job well today.
I feel our **savings cushion** can handle a bad quarter while the mortgage continues.
do: **Lead** the loader crew and check the weekly maintenance sheet by hand.
**Make** the regular mortgage payment and leave emergency savings in place.
feel: **Calm** about limited change, with normal care around family bills.
S0.quote: I have worked this bench long enough to know where the ground gives trouble.
fieldNote: **Experience** and a strong savings cushion make modest AI change feel manageable.
**Manual checking** is a point of professional pride, though she would read a useful fault report.

steps.text: Keep leading loader shifts and checking maintenance sheets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the shift that our old loader still needs a careful operator, even if a report fills itself in. I have worked this bench long enough to know where the ground gives trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not use AI tools, and I would not start just to make a tidy report. My lead pay and our savings cover more than a few months, though the mortgage and two children keep me careful. A normal bad quarter worries me more than this card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the loader crew and check the weekly maintenance sheet by hand. In the first year I would continue the regular mortgage payment and leave the emergency savings alone unless a real bill comes in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. I would rather have ordinary work and ordinary bills than another grand promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much cushion is there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We have more than eight months of basic costs set aside if we cut extras. I earned it by keeping steady shifts, and I do not want it used to chase a new machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the automatic report help the crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it gave the mechanic a clean list of faults, I would read it beside my own notes. I would still sign for the machine only after looking at it.

say: I expect **dispatch** to change before anyone can replace driving on the mine road.
I want **driver numbers** based on tested equipment and actual ground conditions.
think: I see **office tasks** shrinking first and robot trials arriving later.
I trust my **lead role**, but I know a mine can cut shifts unexpectedly.
do: **Keep** the current crew rota while dispatch changes.
**Record** closed ramps and repair delays against new dispatch plans.
**Wait** for a demonstrated machine before changing my own work plan.
feel: **Uneasy** about shift decisions based on software without ground evidence.
S1.quote: I would not resign over a rumour; we have a mortgage to pay.
fieldNote: **Evidence threshold** is high; she wants dated road and repair facts before accepting a changed rota.
**Job security** feels reasonable now, but she knows her senior role does not make a shift immune.

steps.text: Keep the current loader crew rota while dispatch changes
Wait for a demonstrated robot before changing the work plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say dispatch may get quicker at booking trucks, but the road still has to be driven. I would ask that nobody removes a driver from a shift because a plan looks neat on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office may lose tasks first; I can see that. Robots spread more slowly, so my crew should still have work for a while, but I would watch any trial closely. My lead role is strong, yet a mine can reorganise a shift without asking me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep the current crew rota and ask for the written trial schedule before agreeing to a new process. In the first year I would note any actual reduction in driving shifts and wait for a demonstrated machine before changing my own work plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, not frightened. I am more concerned about someone using tidy figures to make a rough shift look simple.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put on the record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would list closed ramps and repair delays against the dispatch plan, with dates. I can explain a delay to management if the facts are written down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if your shifts are cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the mine for the reason and compare openings at the other pits nearby. I would not resign over a rumour; we have a mortgage to pay.

say: I see **2028 thinking AI** changing reports before robots threaten loader shifts around 2031.
I want **trial dates** and expected shift changes given to the crew in writing.
think: I doubt I could master **every system** in only two years.
I know **savings** would buy time if loader hours fell, but not a permanent replacement job.
do: **List** mortgage balance and savings with my partner this month.
**Pay** extra shift income toward the mortgage after 2028, if it comes.
**Ask** the crew representative to seek published robot trial dates.
feel: **Anxious** about possible lost shifts around 2031 and a short time to respond.
S2.quote: The savings buy us time, not another permanent job.
fieldNote: **Resistance to tools** is candid; she does not promise rapid technical retraining.
**Strong savings** softens the shock but does not settle future wages or mortgage payments.
**Crew information** is her chosen collective response: dates, shift counts and safety responsibility.

steps.text: Pay extra shift income toward the mortgage if shifts pay extra
Ask the crew representative to seek written robot trial dates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew the 2028 thinking system will take reports and scheduling before it takes a loader seat. A machine able to handle the ground around 2031 is the part I would take seriously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used AI and I would not pretend I can learn every new system in two years. My experience should matter during the gap, but by 2031 fewer human shifts are possible. The savings buy us time, not another permanent job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would get the mortgage balance and our savings onto one sheet with my partner. In the first year after 2028 I would keep my loader shifts, put any extra shift pay into the mortgage, and ask the crew representative to demand the mine publish its robot trial dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious for the crew and for our household income if machines take shifts around 2031. I can pay the bills for a time, but I do not like the short run-up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the representative to demand?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want trial dates, the number of driving shifts at risk and who signs off safety. We need facts before a skilled operator is told her shift vanished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why pay down the mortgage instead of taking a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not choose a course before I know what jobs the mine will actually keep. Lower debt would give my family more room to decide later.

say: I see **2031 plans** changing before the loader faces capable robots around 2034.
I want a **mine timetable** that shows what happens to lead shifts.
think: I can lower **mortgage debt** with more warning if bonus pay continues.
I could seek **nearby pits** if our lead positions shrink, though I prefer my current crew.
do: **Pay** an extra mortgage instalment from the annual bonus if it arrives.
**Check** posted lead shifts each month after 2031.
**Apply** to two nearby mines if my lead hours fall.
feel: **Uneasy** about eventual crew cuts, with time and local options to respond.
S3.quote: A better title with worse hours would not help our children.
fieldNote: **Bonus dependence** makes her debt plan conditional rather than guaranteed.
**Local options** are real enough to investigate if shifts fall, but she values the known crew.
**Paid instruction** is the minimum she names before operating new equipment.

steps.text: Pay one extra mortgage instalment if the annual bonus arrives
Apply to two nearby mines if lead hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew 2031 changes the reports and plans, while the loader faces those capable robots around 2034. That longer stretch is enough to make the mine show us a real timetable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives us time to reduce the mortgage, but I cannot assume the mine will keep every lead position. I could work at another nearby pit if ours cuts crews, though I would rather stay with people whose habits I know. I am not going to spend our savings on training without a clear job attached.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would pay one extra mortgage instalment from the annual bonus if the bonus comes. In the first year after 2031 I would check the posted shifts each month; if my lead hours fall, I would apply to two nearby mines for equipment lead jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with some control. The extra years mean I can wait for evidence without sitting idle on the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you choose another mine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would call a former coworker at the north pit about its roster, then read the actual job notice. A better title with worse hours would not help our children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the new equipment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would watch a trial from the ground and ask the mechanic what failed. I would operate it only after proper paid instruction and a clear safety sign-off.

say: I want **ten years** used for a proper mine fleet plan, not a last-minute announcement.
I separate **2036 reports** from the possible 2039 change to loader work.
think: I could carry a **smaller mortgage** by age 56 if lead pay continues.
I cannot count on **retirement** before seeing the pension and mortgage figures.
do: **Keep** supervising loader shifts on the current schedule.
**Review** the mortgage balance and savings with my partner each January.
**Compare** the mine fleet plan with our pension statement after 2036.
feel: **Calm** about the near years, while watchful about eventual robot fleets.
S4.quote: Ten years is time to do the sums rather than guess.
fieldNote: **Future ages** are calculated correctly: 53 at thinking AI, 56 at capable robots.
**Senior pay** and strong savings allow a calm near-term response without assuming retirement.
**Pension figures** are required before she would accept fewer shifts.

steps.text: Keep supervising loader shifts on the current schedule
Wait for mine fleet and pension figures before reducing shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a decade gives the mine no excuse to spring a robot fleet on its operators. The thinking systems reach our reports by 2036, and the loader work has until roughly 2039 in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 in 2036 and 56 in 2039. I could have a much smaller mortgage by then if pay remains steady, and nearby mines give me choices. I still would not call retirement certain until I see the pension figure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep supervising loaders and set a mortgage review with my partner every January. In the first year after 2036 I would ask for the mine fleet plan and compare it with our pension statement before accepting fewer shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm for the next few years, with a watchful eye on the far end. Ten years is time to do the sums rather than guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be on the January sheet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would write down the remaining mortgage, savings and the children’s school costs. If the balance is coming down, I would keep the same payment rather than chase a risky investment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What might change your mind about retiring?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A confirmed pension and a paid-off mortgage would make fewer shifts possible. If either number is short, I would keep looking at lead work at nearby mines.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the gap between changed scheduling and capable loader robots is short. Written trial dates and the number of shifts at risk would let us plan without guessing. Mortgage payments would be easier if the mine gave us facts early.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who will teach the younger operators if crews shrink. My experience is useful only if there is time to pass it on before the roster is cut.

headlineQuote: My experience is useful only if there is time to pass it on before the roster is cut.
portrait: **Vera, 43**, leads loader operators at a large mine and trusts ground checks more than polished schedules.
**High pay** and over eight months of basic costs saved give her room to absorb short disruptions while supporting two children.
**Familiar methods** suit her; she never uses AI and demands evidence before accepting new equipment.
**Fast AGI** worries her because reports change by 2028 and capable loader robots may threaten shifts around 2031.
**Longer warning** lets her reduce mortgage debt and inspect nearby mine openings without assuming an early pension.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves the shortest gap between changed scheduling and possible cuts to loader shifts.
whatWouldHelp: **Written robot trial dates** and expected shift numbers would let the crew and her family plan.
